sanlian.1.tier_reason: Common: a reliable hook, but it only works when the consensus is one readers really hold.
sanlian.1.why: Readers nod first and are drawn onto the same side; the takedown that follows shows them they were fooled too, so they read on. The gap between the nod and the surprise is the hook. The precondition is that someone really believes the consensus.
sanlian.1.example: > *Demonstration:* Everyone says the worst thing about renting is a bad landlord. Three years in, I found the worst thing is a landlord who is too good: he brings you vegetables every week, and you cannot bring yourself to say you are moving out.
sanlian.1.breakdown:
- “Everyone says”: the consensus is laid out, and readers agree by default.
- “Three years in, I found”: personal experience backs the takedown, not abstract argument.
- “A landlord who is too good”: the reversal lands on the same object; the subject does not change.
- “Cannot bring yourself to say you are moving out”: a concrete consequence right after the takedown, so the laugh lands.
sanlian.1.overdo:
> As we all know, everyone loves staying up late. But in fact, the essence of staying up late is a longing for freedom.

The problem: the first half is not a consensus at all and the second half is abstract elevation; it knocks down a target that does not exist.
sanlian.1.when_not:
- When you are not sure readers actually share the “consensus”.
- When the piece has already used it once; the second time readers see the trick.
sanlian.1.exercise: Start with “Everyone says early risers are more disciplined” and write three sentences that take it apart through one concrete consequence in daily life.
sanlian.1.check: Show the first sentence alone to a friend. Do they nod? If not, change it.
sanlian.1.adjacent:
- sanlian.8 Doubt and Rebuttal (voices the objection and answers it; false consensus agrees first, then takes apart)
- sanlian.19 Then and Now Couplet (sets old and new ideas side by side, with no need to pretend agreement first)

sanlian.2.tier_reason: Signature: a marker of this style's voice, but memes expire and readers sort by circle.
sanlian.2.why: A meme word carries its own context and mood, so readers get the attitude without explanation; it is also a password for “we scroll the same internet”, which closes the distance fast. The cost is that memes expire and audiences are particular.
sanlian.2.example: > *Demonstration:* Young people looking for a *dazi* (a buddy for one activity) now go all in on a clear division of labor: a meal buddy is for eating, and after the meal nobody looks for anybody.
sanlian.2.breakdown:
- “Go all in on” (the meme pattern *zhuda yige*): the moment it appears, it announces that the tone is a joke.
- “Clear division of labor”: the meme is followed by office vocabulary, two light layers stacked.
- After the colon comes a concrete rule, so the meme is not left hanging.
sanlian.2.overdo:
> This place is all in on being amazing, the vibe is maxed out, instant legend, GOAT.

The problem: meme words piled up with no information; readers finish and still do not know what is good about the place.
sanlian.2.when_not:
- When readers are outside your online circle (older relatives, formal occasions).
- When the meme has passed its window; using it makes you look behind.
sanlian.2.exercise: Pick a meme popular this month and use it to set the tone of “not answering work messages after hours”, in one sentence plus one concrete detail.
sanlian.2.check: Remove the meme word: does the sentence still carry one concrete piece of information? If not, it is an empty meme.
sanlian.2.adjacent:
- sanlian.11 Coinage (makes a new word; this atom borrows a ready-made meme)
- sanlian.13 Meme Archaeology (there the meme is the topic itself; here it only colors one line)

sanlian.3.tier_reason: Core: works across genres and is the first step out of empty language.
sanlian.3.why: Abstract words (“pressure”, “conditions”) are forgotten as soon as they are read; three things you can touch each form a picture in the mind. Three makes a rhythm without turning into a list. This works in any genre and is the first step out of empty language.
sanlian.3.example: > *Demonstration:* What her mother asked about was not what the boyfriend was like as a person, but his mortgage, his social insurance, and how many hours by high-speed train his hometown is from here.
sanlian.3.breakdown:
- “What he was like as a person” is the abstract question being replaced.
- Mortgage, social insurance, hours by train: each covers one dimension, money, security, distance.
- The third item is slightly longer, so the sentence comes to rest there and the rhythm closes naturally.
sanlian.3.overdo:
> We need courage, wisdom and responsibility to embrace change, meet challenges and create the future.

The problem: all three items are abstract, so nothing was replaced; two stacked triads are a classic AI tone.
sanlian.3.when_not:
- When there is only one key object; padding to three dilutes it.
- When the same paragraph has already used one triad.
sanlian.3.exercise: Rewrite “he lives very frugally” as three concrete objects.
sanlian.3.check: Is any of the three items an abstract noun? If so, swap it for something you could photograph.
sanlian.3.adjacent: - sanlian.9 Escalating Gag (three items that rise to make a laugh; here they stand level and replace an abstraction)

sanlian.4.tier_reason: Signature: a defining comic move of this style, easy to tip into real jargon.
sanlian.4.why: The solemnity of the jargon and the triviality of the matter are mismatched, and the mismatch is the joke. Readers are surrounded by these words every day, so moving them into home life lets off some steam on their behalf.
sanlian.4.example: > *Demonstration:* For the weekend family dinner, my mum released a menu requirements document a week in advance, my dad took the procurement side, and I was assigned to the dishwashing post, with no prospect of a permanent contract.
sanlian.4.breakdown:
- “Requirements document”, “procurement side”, “post”: three office terms, each matched to a family role.
- The matter itself is tiny (one meal); the more serious the terms, the funnier.
- “No prospect of a permanent contract”: the last term brings in self-mockery and closes it.
sanlian.4.overdo:
> In a relationship you need top-level design, close the emotional loop, form a replicable methodology, and achieve win-win empowerment.

The problem: term after term with no concrete scene underneath; it reads as genuine corporate jargon.
sanlian.4.when_not:
- When writing about grief, loss or other serious subjects.
- When readers hate these words; overuse makes it sound like you talk that way too.
sanlian.4.exercise: Describe taking turns to take out the dorm rubbish using three office terms, in under 50 words.
sanlian.4.check: Behind each term, can you point to a concrete everyday thing? If not, cut it.
sanlian.4.adjacent: - sanlian.17 Absurd Interpretation (puts technical terms on an object; this atom puts organizational terms on people and events)

sanlian.5.tier_reason: Core: a basic skill for every narrative genre; one micro-scene can stand in for a paragraph of argument.
sanlian.5.why: Seeing a person do something reaches readers far faster than reasoning. A line gives a voice, a turn gives a result. One micro-scene can do the work of a paragraph of argument; it is a basic skill for every kind of narrative writing.
sanlian.5.example: > *Demonstration:* My colleague said my packed lunch was tacky. On the third day at noon she leaned over: “Where did you buy that lunch box?”
sanlian.5.breakdown:
- Person: a colleague, a clear other.
- Turn: from “tacky” to “on the third day she leaned over”; the time phrase completes the flip.
- Line: she only asks about the lunch box and never admits she was won over; the concession hides inside the question.
sanlian.5.overdo:
> In that moment, sunlight fell on her face; she smiled faintly, as if she had understood the meaning of life.

The problem: no line, no turn, only a filter and an elevation. It is a fake scene.
sanlian.5.when_not:
- When the scene is invented and will be taken as true (this style depends on reality).
- In paragraphs that need to explain data or a process.
sanlian.5.exercise: Write a scene of about thirty words: someone goes from objecting to something to quietly starting to do it.
sanlian.5.check: Is there a sentence a person actually says aloud? Is there a change of attitude? Missing either, it does not count.
sanlian.5.adjacent: - sanlian.7 Sample Profile Formula (introduces a real person plus a quote; this atom is a moment in motion)

sanlian.6.tier_reason: Common: gives a piece fixed characters, as long as the label does not offend.
sanlian.6.why: “Some young women” leaves readers cold; one label can be imagined as a specific person and called up again and again. Once a set of labels is in place, the whole piece has a fixed cast.
sanlian.6.example: > *Demonstration:* The “weekend camper” has a fixed kit: a canopy never once put up, a coffee machine, and a folding table that exists to be posted on social media.
sanlian.6.breakdown:
- “Weekend camper”: one label covers a whole group.
- The kit list gives this “person” a character: fussy, fond of showing off, not really camping.
- “Never once put up”: one detail shows the group's endearing side without being cruel.
sanlian.6.overdo:
> Today's workers are generally anxious and drained; they long to be seen yet fear being defined.

The problem: the label is followed by abstract psychology; nobody comes alive, and it turns into a report.
sanlian.6.when_not:
- When the label could carry contempt or offend by region or gender.
- When the group is too niche for readers to recognize.
sanlian.6.exercise: Give “people who read novels on the subway every day” a label and write two concrete habits.
sanlian.6.check: Would the people described laugh at the label or be angry? If angry, change it.
sanlian.6.adjacent:
- sanlian.7 Sample Profile Formula (one real person; this atom is a composite group persona)
- sanlian.11 Coinage (names a phenomenon; this atom names a group of people)

sanlian.7.tier_reason: Common: the most direct source of a living voice, and its lifeline is that the person is real.
sanlian.7.why: A person with a name, a role and their own words turns a phenomenon from “they say” into “it is real”. The quote brings speech and attitude, the most direct source of a living voice. That is why its lifeline is authenticity.
sanlian.7.example: > *Demonstration:* Ajie (a pseudonym), born after 1995 and working in design in a second-tier city, has not bought new clothes in three years: “I've got enough to wear. I'm keeping the money for classes.”
sanlian.7.breakdown:
- “Born after 1995”, “working in design”: tag and role, which help readers place him.
- “(A pseudonym)”: the demonstration states plainly that the name is invented, so it does not pose as a real interview.
- The quote is very short and colloquial; the attitude is clearer than any explanation.
sanlian.7.overdo:
> Xiaomei, a girl born after 2000, says: “I believe that in this fast-paced era, we should learn to make peace with ourselves.”

The problem: the quote is written-up chicken soup; you can tell it is invented, because real people do not talk like that.
sanlian.7.when_not:
- When you have no real interview material. By this engine's rules, change the topic rather than invent names or quotes.
- When one piece has more than four or five samples; readers cannot keep track.
sanlian.7.exercise: Ask someone near you what they think of one spending habit, and write one line using the formula, with the quote unchanged.
sanlian.7.check: Can you say who said this quote and where? If not, cut it.
sanlian.7.adjacent:
- sanlian.6 Group as Person (a composite group)
- sanlian.5 Micro-Scene (a moment of action, not necessarily with identifying details)

sanlian.8.tier_reason: Common: turns a lecture into a conversation, but only against a doubt readers really have.
sanlian.8.why: When readers' objection is said aloud first, they feel the writer understands them. The answer that follows does not hit back; it gives a step and then stands firm, so it reads like conversation, not a lecture.
sanlian.8.example: > *Demonstration:* You can say a folding bike rides like a toy, but don't argue that with someone who saves twenty minutes at the subway entrance every day.
sanlian.8.breakdown:
- “You can say…”: grants that the other side's distaste has a point.
- “But don't argue that with someone who…”: no head-on debate; the say goes to the people who use it.
- “Saves twenty minutes”: answers with one concrete gain, not a grand principle.
sanlian.8.overdo:
> Some people say this is not good, but I want to say that everyone has the right to choose and we should respect diversity.

The problem: the objection is never made concrete and the answer is a correct platitude, so nothing was rebutted.
sanlian.8.when_not:
- When readers do not actually have this doubt; you are setting up your own target.
- When the topic needs serious argument and one light answer does not carry enough weight.
sanlian.8.exercise: Voice the reader's “bullet journals are a waste of time” and answer with one concrete benefit, in two sentences.
sanlian.8.check: Does the answer contain a concrete person or a concrete gain? Attitude alone does not count.
sanlian.8.adjacent:
- sanlian.1 False Consensus (agrees first, then takes apart)
- sanlian.12 Relaxed Close (if the answer lands on “it works for me”, the two often run together)

sanlian.9.tier_reason: Common: a dependable laugh structure, provided the third step really surprises.
sanlian.9.why: The first two steps set a pattern and readers start to expect the next; the third breaks the pattern or blows it up absurdly, and the missed expectation is the laugh. Three is exactly right; one more and it drags.
sanlian.9.example: > *Demonstration:* One person going downstairs in pajamas to collect a parcel is sloppy, two is a coincidence, and the whole building doing it is community culture.
sanlian.9.breakdown:
- The numbers rise: one person, two people, the whole building.
- The verdict shifts: sloppy, coincidence, culture; the third is an absurd promotion.
- The sentence stops at the third step and adds no fourth.
sanlian.9.overdo:
> The first time is an attempt, the second a habit, the third a love, the fourth a faith, the fifth a life.

The problem: five steps, each only swapping a word with no picture, so the laugh thins out into a parallel list.
sanlian.9.when_not:
- When the third step has no surprise; better not to use it.
- When the context already has parallelism; stacking more becomes rhythmic noise.
sanlian.9.exercise: Use “one person… two people… three people…” to write about soaking your feet in the office.
sanlian.9.check: Is the third step surprising? Does it stop at three?
sanlian.9.adjacent:
- sanlian.3 Three Concrete Things (level, not rising)
- sanlian.14 Theory Family (also an extension, but of one named meme)

sanlian.10.tier_reason: Core: a general-purpose way to close any kind of piece.
sanlian.10.why: Meeting a familiar word at the end, readers automatically look back over the piece and feel it has come full circle; the word is the same but its meaning has changed, and the change is the ground the piece has covered. It is a general way to close any kind of writing.
sanlian.10.example: > *Demonstration:* Opening: she said she moved to this city to “live a bit more decently.” Ending: later, the most decent moment she had was on a Sunday afternoon on the balcony, when she finally kept a pot of mint alive.
sanlian.10.breakdown:
- “Decent” appears at the start and at the end.
- At the start, decency means income and status; at the end it lands on a pot of mint, and the meaning has quietly been swapped.
- The ending does not explain the swap; readers make the connection themselves.
sanlian.10.overdo:
> As said at the beginning, dreams matter. Returning to the opening question, we finally understand: dreams really do matter.

The problem: repetition with no change of meaning, and “as said at the beginning” gives the game away; the ring turns into an echo.
sanlian.10.when_not:
- When the opening keyword is not memorable enough for anyone to remember it at the end.
- In pieces shorter than three or four paragraphs, where the ring feels contrived.
sanlian.10.exercise: For a piece about changing jobs, choose an opening word and write one closing sentence that shifts its meaning.
sanlian.10.check: Does the same word at the end mean something different from the start? If not, it is only repetition.
sanlian.10.adjacent: - sanlian.12 Relaxed Close (closes on a scene from daily life; the two often combine, using the scene to complete the ring)

sanlian.11.tier_reason: Common: the name carries the argument, as long as others would actually use it.
sanlian.11.why: Once a phenomenon has a name, readers can use it to point at things around them, and they like to pass it on; the attitude hidden in the name is accepted without argument. The test is whether other people would pick it up.
sanlian.11.example: > *Demonstration:* Sitting in the car for ten extra minutes after work before going upstairs: I call it “garage silent mode”.
sanlian.11.breakdown:
- The phenomenon comes first (ten extra minutes in the car), then the name.
- “Silent mode” borrows a phone setting; the attitude is to legitimize, not mock.
- The name is short, easy to say, and can be used in speech straight away.
sanlian.11.overdo:
> I call this phenomenon “postmodern emotional self-boundary reconstruction syndrome”.

The problem: the name is long and awkward; even the writer cannot say it smoothly, and readers will not pass it on.
sanlian.11.when_not:
- When the phenomenon already has an accepted name; renaming only causes confusion.
- More than two coinages in one piece; readers cannot remember them.
sanlian.11.exercise: Coin a short name, two to four words, for starting to dread Monday on Sunday evening.
sanlian.11.check: Say the name to a friend: can they guess what it means without explanation?
sanlian.11.adjacent:
- sanlian.2 Meme as Verb (borrows a ready-made meme)
- sanlian.14 Theory Family (extends one name into a series)

sanlian.12.tier_reason: Core: the defining close of this style, and its sharpest difference from official prose.
sanlian.12.why: After laughing and chatting, a sudden lofty ending makes readers feel lectured. Landing back on a meal or an afternoon lets them leave with that picture and keeps the judgment in their hands. This is the biggest difference between this living voice and official prose: no verdict.
sanlian.12.example: > *Demonstration:* As for whether to buy that oven, I haven't decided. Anyway, tonight the pancake stall downstairs is still open.
sanlian.12.breakdown:
- “Haven't decided”: deliberately gives up offering an answer.
- “Tonight”, “the pancake stall downstairs”: time and place are both close and small.
- The tone is light, with not one evaluative word.
sanlian.12.overdo:
> Life is more than the grind in front of us; may we all live with ease and be the protagonists of our own lives.

The problem: it talks about ease while shouting a slogan, which is exactly what this atom avoids.
sanlian.12.when_not:
- When the piece must give readers clear advice (such as a guide to avoiding pitfalls).
- When writing about serious loss, where a light close reads as flippant.
sanlian.12.exercise: Write the ending of a short piece on whether to sit the postgraduate exam, using only a picture from that day's life.
sanlian.12.check: Does the last paragraph contain advice words like “should”, “may you” or “must”? If so, cut them.
sanlian.12.adjacent:
- sanlian.20 Humble Aphorism (closes on a line; this atom closes on a scene)
- sanlian.10 Ring Structure (can be combined)

sanlian.13.tier_reason: Signature: a topic type unique to this style, and it depends on the meme's moment.
sanlian.13.why: Readers see the meme every day without knowing where it came from, and archaeology satisfies that curiosity. Following who uses it turns the meme from a joke into a mirror. It depends on the meme's moment; too late and it is reheated leftovers.
sanlian.13.example: > *Demonstration:* “E-pickles” (a video you keep playing while you eat, the way pickles help rice go down) started with people who had to have a video on to get through a meal. Later it came to cover more and more, even a podcast on the commute. The people who use the word mostly eat alone.
sanlian.13.breakdown:
- Source: one concrete eating scene.
- Spread: the range of use widens, showing the meme is growing.
- Users: “mostly eat alone” points to the mindset without passing judgment.
sanlian.13.overdo:
> The phrase “lying flat” has gone viral online, reflecting deep shifts in the social psychology and values of contemporary youth.

The problem: no archaeology, straight to editorial elevation; the meme is only a pretext.
sanlian.13.when_not:
- When the meme has passed the two-to-three-week window after it took off.
- When you cannot find a reliable source; do not invent an origin story.
sanlian.13.exercise: Pick this week's hot meme and write three sentences: where it came from, who uses it, and what they get from it.
sanlian.13.check: For the source sentence, can you give a verifiable origin? If not, rewrite it as “reportedly” or pick another meme.
sanlian.13.adjacent:
- sanlian.14 Theory Family (archaeology is often followed by a family)
- sanlian.2 Meme as Verb (borrows the meme without digging into it)

sanlian.14.tier_reason: Signature: a characteristic way this style stretches one meme, effective only once or twice.
sanlian.14.why: Once readers recognize the template, the second sibling gets a knowing smile, like a word-chain game; the family can also sort the phenomenon into types along the way. But the second one works; from the third on it is padding.
sanlian.14.example: > *Demonstration:* Once there are “e-pickles”, there will be “e-salted-veg”: old dramas that help the rice go down but get cloying after a while. And “e-plain-congee”: the white noise you put on when you don't feel like watching anything.
sanlian.14.breakdown:
- Fixed template: “e- plus a side dish that helps rice go down”.
- Each sibling matches a real type of content, not an empty word chain.
- It stops after two.
sanlian.14.overdo:
> E-pickles, e-salted-veg, e-kimchi, e-fermented-tofu, e-chili-sauce, e-Lao-Gan-Ma…

The problem: only the noun changes, with nothing it maps to; the chain is just filling space.
sanlian.14.when_not:
- When the original meme has not settled and readers do not yet know the template.
- When you have already extended it twice.
sanlian.14.exercise: Using *dazi* (activity buddy) as the template, extend two new kinds of buddy, each with one concrete line of explanation.
sanlian.14.check: Can each family member be matched to a real phenomenon readers recognize?
sanlian.14.adjacent:
- sanlian.11 Coinage (a single new word)
- sanlian.9 Escalating Gag (rises to make a laugh; this atom extends in parallel)

sanlian.15.tier_reason: Common: a signpost for skim readers, as long as material backs it up.
sanlian.15.why: Phone reading is skimming; a bold line standing alone gets seen first, so readers catch the point at a glance and can screenshot and share it. It is a signpost for skimmers, and it needs material behind it.
sanlian.15.example:
> *Demonstration:*
>
> **Anyone who can keep a pothos alive has already beaten most weekends.**
>
> Only then: she has moved house three times, and that pothos is the one thing that has come with her all the way.
sanlian.15.breakdown:
- The line has a concrete object (the pothos); it is not pure abstraction.
- On its own line and in bold, it catches the eye first.
- Concrete material follows immediately, so the line is not left hanging.
sanlian.15.overdo:
> **No road in life is walked in vain; every step counts.**

The problem: one-size-fits-all chicken soup; the bold only magnifies the emptiness.
sanlian.15.when_not:
- More than two or three in one piece, and the bold stops standing out.
- When nothing later in the piece backs it up.
sanlian.15.exercise: Write a stand-alone line about eating hotpot alone; it must contain one concrete object.
sanlian.15.check: Swap the topic: does the line still hold? If it does, it is too empty and needs work.
sanlian.15.adjacent:
- sanlian.16 Short Spoken Assertion (shorter and more spoken, no bold needed)
- sanlian.20 Humble Aphorism (goes at the close and lowers the stance)

sanlian.16.tier_reason: Common: a quick rhythmic beat, effective only after a longer build-up.
sanlian.16.why: After a long build-up, a short sentence stops the rhythm, like someone slapping the table mid-sentence; being spoken, it sounds less like a lecture and more like a friend making the decision for you. It works through contrast: the long sentences drag readers into hesitation, comparison and back-and-forth, and the short one cuts straight through at the peak of the dithering. The tension drops at once, and that release is the laugh. The full stop matters too: an exclamation mark turns decisiveness into shouting, a question mark sends resolve back into doubt; only the full stop says “done, no discussion”.
sanlian.16.example: > *Demonstration:* A whole evening of agonizing over which colour of phone case to get. In the end, eyes shut, one tap. Whatever it lands on.
sanlian.16.breakdown:
- “A whole evening of agonizing over which colour of phone case to get”: a long sentence; “a whole evening” stretches the dithering to the full, and “phone case” makes its object comically small, so the build-up already carries a contrast.
- “In the end, eyes shut, one tap.”: medium length, the bridge from long to short; the rhythm starts to tighten.
- “Whatever it lands on.”: four words closed by a full stop; it is the spoken way of settling it, gives no reason at all, and that is exactly what shows resolve.
- The three sentences shrink in length, long, medium, short; that drop is the skeleton of this atom.
sanlian.16.overdo:
> No more self-drain. Embrace growth. Be yourself. Never settle. Charge ahead.

The problem: short sentences fired in a row, all slogans, with no build-up before them; only a wall of banners is left.
sanlian.16.when_not:
- When there is no build-up before it; the short line has no pause to create.
- Three or more in a row.
sanlian.16.exercise: Write about 40 words of dithering, then close with an assertion of six words or fewer.
sanlian.16.check: Is there a sentence much longer than the assertion just before it?
sanlian.16.adjacent:
- sanlian.15 Pull-Quote Line (states the point and can be longer)
- sanlian.20 Humble Aphorism (at the close, carrying a lesson)

sanlian.17.tier_reason: Signature: this style's straight-faced joke, which must stay obviously a joke.
sanlian.17.why: The more homely the object and the more technical the term, the bigger the gap; readers know it is nonsense yet are amused by the earnest tone. At bottom it is a joke told with a straight face.
sanlian.17.example: > *Demonstration:* Carrying two big bags of groceries up five floors every day is defined in our house as “loaded aerobic plus lower-body compound strength training”, with my mum as head coach.
sanlian.17.breakdown:
- Everyday action: carrying groceries upstairs.
- Technical terms: fitness training vocabulary, funnier the more precise it is.
- “My mum as head coach”: the absurdity extends to a person and closes inside the family.
sanlian.17.overdo:
> Daydreaming is actually the brain carrying out deep cognitive restructuring and neuroplasticity optimization, which is very scientific.

The problem: the tone is genuinely explanatory, and readers cannot tell whether it is a joke or misinformation.
sanlian.17.when_not:
- In health, medicine and other areas where readers might take it seriously.
- When readers need accurate information.
sanlian.17.exercise: Use one technical term to “interpret” hanging out the washing, in two sentences.
sanlian.17.check: Can readers tell at once that this is a joke? If not, it becomes misinformation.
sanlian.17.adjacent:
- sanlian.4 Borrowed Jargon (applies organizational terms)
- sanlian.18 Pop-Science Seasoning (half-true popular science, mentioned in passing)

sanlian.18.tier_reason: Signature: a flavour typical of this style that must never carry the argument.
sanlian.18.why: Readers have heard these words, so a mention brings a light sense of “there might be something to that” and a playful touch of knowledge. But it cannot bear weight: the moment a reader asks which study, the piece collapses.
sanlian.18.example: > *Demonstration:* Buying a milk tea on the way home from work is like sending my dopamine a little red envelope. Whether that is scientific, I'll drink first and worry later.
sanlian.18.breakdown:
- “Dopamine” is mentioned in passing; the mechanism is not explained.
- “A little red envelope” pulls the science word back into an everyday image.
- “I'll drink first and worry later”: deliberately backs down, declaring that it is not evidence.
sanlian.18.overdo:
> Research shows that drinking milk tea every day significantly increases happiness by 37%, so milk tea is a necessity.

The problem: an invented study and figure, then used as the basis for a conclusion. That is exactly this atom's red line.
sanlian.18.when_not:
- When the point really needs evidence; cite a reliable source, not a meme.
- When it involves health advice.
sanlian.18.exercise: In one sentence about sleeping in at the weekend, add a popular science word and make fun of yourself for its lack of rigour.
sanlian.18.check: Delete the science word: does the point still stand? If not, you are making it bear weight.
sanlian.18.adjacent:
- sanlian.17 Absurd Interpretation (an obvious joke)
- sanlian.13 Meme Archaeology (digs into memes, not science)

sanlian.19.tier_reason: Common: compresses a change of era into one line, as long as both sides are concrete.
sanlian.19.why: With two ideas side by side, readers see the change without argument; the paired structure gives the change rhythm and makes it memorable. It squeezes a shift of era into one sentence.
sanlian.19.example: > *Demonstration:* Lunar New Year face used to mean eighteen dishes on one table; now face means who finishes the washing-up first after the reunion dinner.
sanlian.19.breakdown:
- “Used to / now”: the two poles laid out.
- The same word, “face”, points to a concrete thing on each side.
- The new idea lands on something smaller and more practical; the attitude hides in the contrast.
sanlian.19.overdo:
> In the past we pursued material things; now we pursue the spiritual. In the past we looked outward; now we seek within.

The problem: both sides are abstract; neatly paired but empty, like a slogan.
sanlian.19.when_not:
- When the change is not obvious; a forced contrast distorts it.
- When the contrast implies looking down on a generation.
sanlian.19.exercise: Use “used to… now…” to describe how class reunions have changed, with one concrete object on each side.
sanlian.19.adjacent:
- sanlian.1 False Consensus (takes one idea apart)
- sanlian.3 Three Concrete Things (makes the same demand for concreteness)

sanlian.20.tier_reason: Common: a low-key close that reads as honest, but it needs a high goal set up earlier.
sanlian.20.why: Readers are on guard against lofty lessons and have no defence against “just doing the basics is enough”. The lower the stance, the more it sounds true, with a layer of self-mocking humour on top.
sanlian.20.example: > *Demonstration:* After a year of every kind of self-discipline plan, I finally realised that anyone who takes the rubbish down on time every day is already doing remarkably well.
sanlian.20.breakdown:
- “After a year of every kind of plan”: first, the high goal that failed.
- “Takes the rubbish down on time”: the standard pressed down to the floor.
- “Remarkably well”: praising a small thing in an inflated tone, which makes the humour.
sanlian.20.overdo:
> Ordinariness is the only answer; may you and I all become ordinary yet great people.

The problem: it talks about being ordinary while the sentence climbs; a fake low stance.
sanlian.20.when_not:
- When nothing earlier sets up a high goal; the low stance has nothing to stand out against.
- When the piece already closes on a scene; one more line is redundant.
sanlian.20.exercise: Write a humble line about a reading plan, with a standard so low it is funny.
sanlian.20.check: Is the standard low enough that anyone could meet it? It should be.
sanlian.20.adjacent:
- sanlian.12 Relaxed Close (closes on a scene)
- sanlian.15 Pull-Quote Line (goes at the start to state the point)

sanlian.21.tier_reason: Signature: headline-grade wordplay typical of this style, and easy to force.
sanlian.21.why: Readers take in one meaning, then catch the second, and that moment of catching on is the laugh; a pun also suits headlines, packing two pieces of information into the fewest words. In a good pun the two meanings usually pull opposite ways: the first is the familiar everyday sense and sets an expectation; the second splits or repurposes the word and lands on a more awkward, more real situation, gently turning the expectation over. Readers recognise themselves in the turn and laugh with a little self-mockery, which is the effect this living voice wants. A pun also filters its audience: those who get the second layer feel “this is about me” and want to share it.
sanlian.21.example:
> *Demonstration:* Headline: “Young people are taking up *yangsheng*: first make a living, then worry about the rest.”
>
> (*Yangsheng* 养生 normally means looking after your health; read as 养 + 生, “keep” + “livelihood”, it means scraping a living.)
sanlian.21.breakdown:
- First layer of *yangsheng*: health care. Readers think of goji berries and early nights and expect a health piece.
- Second layer: “make a living”. The word is split into “keep” plus “livelihood”, and the situation drops from caring for the body to staying afloat.
- Quotation marks around the word signal that it is being used another way: do not read it only literally.
- The subtitle spells out the second layer so readers do not miss it; “then worry about the rest” closes in speech and makes the hardship sound light.
- The whole headline has one pun; the rest is plain speech, so the joke stays focused.
sanlian.21.overdo:
> A three-part headline where every phrase forces a pun on a workplace word (salary, job, position) into a stock romantic idiom.

The problem: homophones jammed in, each more strained than the last; readers just feel tired.
sanlian.21.when_not:
- When the pun takes ages to explain.
- On serious subjects, where a pun looks disrespectful.
sanlian.21.exercise: Think of a pun headline for a piece about renting, using only one punning word.
sanlian.21.check: Do both meanings relate to the content of the piece? If only one does, it is forced.
sanlian.21.adjacent:
- sanlian.2 Meme as Verb (borrows a meme to set the tone)
- sanlian.11 Coinage (makes a new word rather than playing on two meanings of one)
